course: NISM Series II-B: Registrars to an Issue and Share Transfer Agents - Mutual Fund
overview: This chapter is all about 'Equity', which simply means ownership. If Unit 1 taught you that there are different buckets to put your money in, this chapter explains the most popular and rewarding bucket: Shares (Equity). As an RTA (Registrar and Transfer Agent), you will be dealing heavily with equity mutual funds. To understand how an equity mutual fund works, you first need to perfectly understand how a single equity share works, how it makes money for the investor, the risks involved, and the different values attached to a share.

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: Buying an equity share means you are buying a small piece of ownership in a company. You become a part-owner (shareholder).
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation: When a company like Tata Motors needs a large amount of money (capital) to build a new factory, they divide their total capital requirement into small, equal parts. Each small part is called a 'Share'. People who buy these shares are called shareholders. Because you are an owner, your money is now permanent capital for the company—they will not return your investment amount to you directly (unless the company shuts down). Instead, if you want your money back, you must sell your shares to someone else in the stock market. As an owner, you also get 'Voting Rights', meaning you can vote on important company decisions during their Annual General Meeting (AGM). However, you take the maximum risk. If the company fails, you lose your money. If it succeeds, you get unlimited profit potential.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: For the exam, you must know the legal rights of an equity shareholder. RTAs maintain the exact list of who owns these shares and who is eligible to vote.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: If Reliance Industries has 100 crore total shares, and you buy 100 shares, you literally own a very tiny, fractional percentage of the entire Reliance empire.
exam_traps: Exam Trap: 'Equity shareholders have a guaranteed fixed return.' False! They get what is left over after paying everyone else (Residual claim).
Exam Trap: 'Companies must refund equity capital after 5 years.' False! Equity is permanent capital.
Remember that Equity shareholders are the LAST to be paid if a company goes bankrupt.
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: Equity = Equal partner in Profit and Pain. You own it, you vote on it, you take the risk.

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: You make money from shares in two ways: 1) The company shares its profits with you (Dividend). 2) The price of the share goes up (Capital Appreciation).
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
Step 1: Dividend. When a company does business and makes a net profit, it can choose to distribute a portion of that profit to its shareholders. This cash reward is called a Dividend. It is not mandatory; if the company wants to use the profit to grow the business instead, it can skip the dividend. 
Step 2: Capital Appreciation. This is the main reason people buy shares. If the company is growing and making more profit, more people will want to buy its shares. High demand pushes the share price up in the stock market. If you bought it at a low price and sell it at a high price, the difference is your profit (Capital Gain/Appreciation).
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: Mutual funds calculate their Net Asset Value (NAV) based on the capital appreciation of the shares they hold. Also, dividend processing is a core duty of an RTA.
complete_concept_explanation.formula: Total Return = Dividend Received + (Selling Price - Purchase Price)
complete_concept_explanation.formula_explanation: Your total profit is the cash you received while holding the share (dividend) plus the profit you made when you sold it.
complete_concept_explanation.step_by_step_calculation_example:
Step 1: You buy 1 share of Infosys at Rs. 1,000.
Step 2: During the year, Infosys pays a dividend of Rs. 30 directly into your bank account.
Step 3: After 1 year, the share price goes up to Rs. 1,200. You sell it.
Step 4: Capital Appreciation = 1,200 - 1,000 = Rs. 200.
Step 5: Total Return = Rs. 200 (Capital Gain) + Rs. 30 (Dividend) = Rs. 230 total profit.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: Companies like ITC or Coal India are famous for giving high, regular 'Dividends'. Companies like Zomato or DMart usually don't pay dividends; investors buy them purely for 'Capital Appreciation' expecting the price to double or triple over time.
exam_traps: Paying dividends is NEVER legally mandatory for a company. It is decided by the Board of Directors.
Dividends are declared as a percentage of FACE VALUE, never on the Market Value. (This is the most frequently asked NISM trap!)
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: Returns = Daily Milk (Dividend) + Selling the Fat Cow (Capital Appreciation).

complete_concept_explanation.concept: 3. Face Value vs. Book Value vs. Market Value
complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: A single share has three different price tags. Face Value is the original birth price. Book Value is what the share is worth on the company's accounting books today. Market Value is what people are willing to pay for it today on the stock exchange.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
1. Face Value (Par Value): This is the original price at which the company first created the share. It is written on the share certificate. It rarely changes (unless there is a stock split). Usually, it is Rs. 1, Rs. 2, Rs. 5, or Rs. 10 in India. 
2. Book Value: If the company decides to shut down today, sells all its factories and assets, and pays off all its bank loans (liabilities), whatever money is left belongs to shareholders. Divide this left-over money by the total number of shares, and you get the Book Value. It's the 'real' internal accounting value.
3. Market Value: This is the current trading price on the NSE or BSE. It changes every second based on demand and supply, news, and future expectations. It is usually much higher than the Book Value.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: RTAs must track the Face Value for corporate actions. The NISM exam heavily tests your ability to distinguish these three values, especially regarding how dividends are calculated.
complete_concept_explanation.formula: Book Value per share = (Total Assets - Total Liabilities) / Total Number of Outstanding Shares
complete_concept_explanation.formula_explanation: Assets are what the company owns. Liabilities are what it owes. The difference is the 'Net Worth' belonging to the owners. Divide Net Worth by total shares to find the value of one share on the books.
complete_concept_explanation.step_by_step_calculation_example:
Step 1: A company declares a 50% dividend.
Step 2: The share's Market Value is Rs. 2,000.
Step 3: The share's Face Value is Rs. 10.
Step 4: Question: How much dividend do you get per share?
Step 5: Calculation: 50% of Face Value (Rs. 10) = Rs. 5 per share. 
(Do NOT calculate 50% of Rs. 2000! You will get it wrong!).
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: MRF Tyres has a Face Value of Rs. 10. Its Book Value might be around Rs. 35,000. But its Market Value (what you pay to buy it on NSE) is over Rs. 1,00,000! They are all different.
exam_traps: TRAP: 'Company declares 100% dividend on a share trading at Rs. 500. Investor gets Rs. 500.' FALSE! The dividend is 100% of the FACE VALUE (e.g., Rs. 10).
Market value can be lower than book value if a company is doing very badly and making heavy losses.
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: Face Value = Birth Certificate Price. Book Value = Accounting Price. Market Value = Public Demand Price.

complete_concept_explanation.basic_meaning: These are major events initiated by the company that bring changes to the shares you hold. RTAs are the main agencies that execute these actions.
complete_concept_explanation.detailed_explanation:
1. Bonus Issue: The company gives free extra shares to existing shareholders out of its accumulated profits. For example, a 1:1 bonus means for every 1 share you hold, you get 1 free share. Your number of shares doubles, but the market price usually halves. 
2. Stock Split: The company literally cuts one share into smaller pieces. A Rs. 10 Face Value share might be split into ten Rs. 1 Face Value shares. You now have 10 shares instead of 1, but the Face Value drops. This is done to make the share price cheaper and more affordable for small investors. 
3. Rights Issue: The company needs fresh money. Instead of going to the public, it offers new shares to its *existing* shareholders first, usually at a discount to the market price. It is your 'Right' to buy them, not an obligation.
complete_concept_explanation.why_this_is_important: This is the bread-and-butter work of an RTA. When a mutual fund holds shares, and a Bonus is declared, the RTA must ensure the mutual fund gets those extra shares accurately.
complete_concept_explanation.step_by_step_calculation_example:
Stock Split Example: You own 100 shares of a company trading at Rs. 5,000 each (Face value Rs. 10). Total investment = Rs. 5,00,000. 
The company announces a 1-for-5 split (Face value becomes Rs. 2). 
New holding: You now have 500 shares. The market price will adjust to Rs. 1,000. 
Total investment remains the same: 500 x 1,000 = Rs. 5,00,000. Nothing changed in your wealth, you just have more 'pieces' of the pizza.
complete_concept_explanation.real_life_indian_example: IRCTC did a stock split where they changed the face value from Rs. 10 to Rs. 2. The share price dropped proportionally, making it cheaper for retail investors to buy.
exam_traps: Trap: Does a Bonus issue or Stock Split make you richer immediately? NO. The number of shares increases, but the market price falls proportionately. Total value remains the same.
Crucial Difference: In a Bonus issue, the Face Value remains the SAME. In a Stock Split, the Face Value is REDUCED.
Rights issue brings fresh money into the company. Bonus and Split do NOT bring any new money to the company.
complete_concept_explanation.memory_trick: Bonus = Free shares, Face Value unchanged. Split = Chopping shares, Face Value reduced. Rights = Discounted shares, new money raised.

important_differences.clear_explanation: In a Bonus Issue, the company gives free shares from its reserves; the Face Value of the share remains unchanged. In a Stock Split, the company simply divides the existing shares into smaller units to make them affordable; the Face Value reduces proportionately. Neither event changes the fundamental value of your total investment immediately.

Equity shares have voting rights but no guaranteed dividend (highest risk, highest return). Preference shares usually do NOT have voting rights, but they get a fixed percentage of dividend, and they get paid their dividend BEFORE equity shareholders get anything (lower risk, limited return).

Face Value is the static, nominal value assigned when the share is first issued (used to calculate dividends). Market Value is the dynamic, ever-changing price at which the share trades on the stock exchange (based on supply and demand).

frequently_asked_exam_areas: Dividend calculation trap (Always calculate on Face Value, never Market Value).
Identifying who has the 'Residual Claim' (Equity shareholders get paid last during liquidation).
The exact difference between a Bonus issue and a Stock Split regarding Face Value changes.
Understanding that companies are under no legal obligation to declare a dividend.
quick_revision_summary: Equity represents permanent ownership and voting rights in a company.
Returns from equity come from Dividends (sharing profit) and Capital Appreciation (price increase).
Dividends are strictly calculated as a percentage of the Face Value.
Book Value is Net Assets divided by total shares (the internal accounting worth).
Bonus issues keep Face Value the same; Stock Splits reduce Face Value; Rights issues bring fresh capital from existing investors.
Equity investors take maximum risk because they have a residual claim (paid last) if the company closes.
